\title{Can Epidemic Mechanics Guide Graph Networks? SEIR-Informed Spatio-Temporal Forecasting of Weekly Dengue in Sri Lanka}

% Venue: ICITR, University of Moratuwa. User-specified maximum: 6 pages including references.
\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Tharusha Perera, Praveen De Silva, Janith Mahanama,\\
Bimsara Udurawana, Maleesha Kumarasinghe, Praveen Nawarathna}

\begin{abstract}
Graph neural networks can share information between neighbouring districts, but they know nothing about how a dengue infection progresses.
We propose an SEIR-informed spatio-temporal graph network that passes a learned district graph into a decoder running a susceptible--exposed--infectious--recovered (SEIR) simulator.
The decoder's force of infection is scaled by district population and susceptible fraction, its initial exposed fraction is learned, and a learned gate blends its forecast with last week's count.
We evaluate the model on a rebuilt series of 559 weekly reports for 25 Sri Lankan districts, three weeks ahead. % EV-216, EV-007
Rebuilding the series exposed a formula error in one published source table; on the earlier benchmark array, that single week moves the error of the persistence baseline from 44.80 to 29.52 cases per district-week. % EV-220
Across nine rolling forecast origins, the proposed model has the lowest test error of 30 compared models, 27.45 against 28.54 for persistence (paired difference -1.10, 95\% interval -2.84 to 0.65). % EV-200, EV-215
Scaling the force of infection by population lowers the error of a gated SEIR head from 28.43 to 27.62 on the same graph encoder. % EV-210, EV-213
No difference from persistence is significant after adjustment for multiple comparisons, and a graph network with a residual head reaches 28.12. % EV-202, EV-219
The mechanistic decoder therefore makes epidemic structure usable inside a graph network, but nine origins cannot yet show that it beats a strong simple baseline.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
dengue forecasting, epidemic modeling, graph neural networks, persistence baseline, physics-informed learning, SEIR model
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
Dengue causes recurring epidemics in Sri Lanka~\cite{tissera2020severe}.
Forecasts of weekly cases for each district, a few weeks ahead, could help health officers plan clinical capacity and vector control.
Spatio-temporal graph neural networks are a natural choice, because neighbouring districts exchange infections and share reporting patterns~\cite{weng2024graph}.
They learn only from past counts, however, and nothing in them encodes the incubation and recovery that shape an epidemic curve.

Compartmental models carry exactly that knowledge.
An SEIR model tracks how people move from susceptible to exposed, infectious and recovered, and Liu et al.~\cite{liu2025seirlstm} showed that an LSTM can learn its force of infection for Sri Lankan dengue.
We ask whether the same mechanism helps a graph network: does an SEIR decoder on top of a graph encoder forecast weekly district counts better than the encoder alone, and better than repeating last week's count?
Persistence is the reference that matters most, because weekly counts change slowly; the benchmark this work builds on does not report it~\cite{weng2024graph}.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item An SEIR-informed graph network: an adaptive graph encoder, a gated SEIR decoder whose force of infection is anchored to district population and susceptible fraction, and a learned initial exposed fraction.
\item An evaluation on a rebuilt and source-checked district series with nine rolling forecast origins, paired tests, and intervals against persistence, a graph baseline, and published spatio-temporal encoders.
\item Ablations that show what the mechanistic decoder contributes (free versus anchored rate, bare versus gated head, mass-action variant) and a measurement of how a source-table error changes the baseline.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related Work}
Weng et al.~\cite{weng2024graph} adapt graph encoders for Sri Lankan dengue forecasting and compare STGAT, A3T-GCN, ASTGCN, DCRNN, and AAGCN, which use graph attention, temporal attention, spatial-temporal attention, diffusion recurrence, and adaptive graph convolution~\cite{huang2019stgat,bai2021a3tgcn,guo2019astgcn,li2018dcrnn,shi2019aagcn}.
Our STGAT follows their dengue adaptation, not the original pedestrian-trajectory model.
DengueGNN also studies graph-based dengue prediction~\cite{gulmohamed2026denguegnn}, and Graph WaveNet supplies the learned-adjacency construction of our adaptive encoder~\cite{wu2019graphwavenet}.
Liu et al.~\cite{liu2025seirlstm} learn a force of infection for a human SEIR model of Sri Lankan dengue with an LSTM.
EINNs and CausalGNN place epidemiological structure inside neural forecasters, and MepoGNN couples graph learning with metapopulation dynamics~\cite{rodriguez2023einns,wang2022causalgnn,cao2023mepognn}.
We combine the two lines: a graph encoder with an SEIR decoder, tested against persistence on the same district series.

\section{Data}\label{sec:data}
The rebuilt series contains 559 weekly reports for 25 districts, from June 15, 2013, to February 24, 2024; seven reports are missing and are never filled. % EV-216
Any forecast window whose inputs or targets touch a missing report is dropped.
The task maps three past weeks of counts to the next three weeks. % EV-007
The earlier benchmark array, which we call the legacy array, has 459 rows and no verified calendar. % EV-002

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_data.pdf}
\caption{National weekly cases (sum over 25 districts). (a) Legacy benchmark array, by row; the marked row comes from a published table with a formula error. (b) Rebuilt series used in this study; gaps are missing reports.}
\label{fig:data}
\end{figure}

While rebuilding the series we checked every district row against the printed national total.
Legacy row 395 comes from the report for December 26, 2020, to January 1, 2021~\cite{epid2021wer0248}. % EV-222
In its weekly row, 15 of 24 inner cells equal the sum of the two cells before them, and the districts sum to 7165 while the printed national total is 35. % EV-222
The same table's year-to-date row, which equals the weekly count in the first week of a year, sums with the Kalmunai division to the printed total of 351. % EV-222
The spike in Fig.~\ref{fig:data}a is therefore a spreadsheet error, not an outbreak, and the rebuilt series uses the year-to-date row.

Districts are nodes of a graph whose edges are shared borders.
Checking the border list against GADM polygons gives 57 shared borders, 114 directed entries, and 139 entries with self-loops. % EV-221
The graph used in the experiments below came from the benchmark and lists two further one-directional entries (Kandy to Ampara, Kegalle to Kalutara) that are not borders, 141 entries in total. % EV-221

\section{SEIR-Informed Graph Network}\label{sec:methods}
Fig.~\ref{fig:arch} shows the model.
A graph encoder turns the input window into a representation per district, a read-out gives one value $r$ per district and horizon, and a head turns $r$ into a forecast, either directly or through an SEIR simulator.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_arch.pdf}
\caption{SEIR-informed graph network. The encoder and read-out feed either a non-SEIR head or an SEIR head that converts a force of infection into weekly incidence through daily compartment flows. The last observed week is the anchor of the residual and gated heads; district population and initial compartments enter the SEIR head. The dashed path is used only in training.}
\label{fig:arch}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{Encoder and heads}
Counts $c_{i,t}$ for district $i$ and week $t$ are standardized with training-period statistics,
\begin{equation}
z_{i,t}=\{\log(1+c_{i,t})-\mu\}/\sigma.
\label{eq:z}
\end{equation}
% seirgnn2/core.py::build_tensors
The persistence anchor $p$ repeats the standardized latest count for every horizon.
The GCN encoder projects the input to 64 dimensions and applies two residual graph layers, $H' = H+\mathrm{Dropout}(\mathrm{ReLU}(AHW+b))$, with $A$ the row-normalized border adjacency with self-loops. % EV-177
% seirgnn2/models.py::GraphLayer, Net.encode; seirgnn2/core.py::adjacency
The adaptive encoder learns $A_{\rm ad}=\mathrm{softmax}(\mathrm{ReLU}(E_1E_2^\top))$ from standard-normal $25\times10$ node embeddings shared by both layers and exempt from weight decay. % EV-177
% seirgnn2/models.py::learned_adjacency, adaptive_embeddings; seirgnn2/train.py::_optimizer
Published encoders can replace this stage.
The direct, residual, and gated non-SEIR heads output $r$, $p+r$, and $p+g(r-p)$, with gate $g=\mathrm{sigmoid}(a)$ and $a$ initialized at $-2$. % EV-178
The bare SEIR head outputs the standardized simulator count $z(\hat c)$, and the gated SEIR head outputs $p+g\{z(\hat c)-p\}$.
% seirgnn2/models.py::Net.forward
Training minimizes squared error on the standardized log scale; its minimizer is the conditional mean of $\log(1+c)$, which, transformed back, is not the count-scale mean that RMSE rewards.

\subsection{SEIR decoder}
The decoder advances the susceptible, exposed, infectious, and recovered fractions of each district one day at a time with exponential flows,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
f_S&=S(1-e^{-\lambda\Delta t}),\quad f_E=E(1-e^{-\omega\Delta t}),\\
f_I&=I(1-e^{-\gamma\Delta t}),\quad
\hat c_{i,h}=\rho_{\rm eff}N_i\sum_{d=1}^{7} f_E^{(d)}.
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:seir}
\end{equation}
% analysis/lib/seir_sim.py::_step, simulate_weeks; seirgnn2/models.py::Net._physics
Flows are computed from the current state and moved along $S\rightarrow E\rightarrow I\rightarrow R$; the weekly count is the sum of daily exposed-to-infectious flows, times the district population $N_i$ and an effective reporting fraction.
The rates are $\omega=0.7/7=0.1$ and $\gamma=1/7$ per day with seven daily steps, mean exposed and infectious periods of ten and seven days, following Liu et al.~\cite{liu2025seirlstm}. % EV-011
The base reporting fraction $\rho=1/11$ follows the same work, and a learned scalar $q$ gives $\rho_{\rm eff}=\rho\exp(q)$. % EV-011, EV-217
Initial infectious and exposed fractions come from $c_{t-1}/(\rho N_i)$ and $c_{t-2}/(\rho N_i)$, clipped to $[10^{-6},0.5]$. % EV-170
The susceptible fraction is $\mathrm{clip}(0.318-C_{<t}/(\rho N_i),0.01,1)$, where $C_{<t}$ is the sum of earlier reports. % EV-170
The value 0.318 is one minus the 68.2\% seroprevalence measured in suburban Colombo~\cite{jeewandara2015sero}, applied to every district. % EV-170, EV-223
A learned multiplier $2\,\mathrm{sigmoid}(v)$ rescales the exposed fraction, either globally or per district from the encoder (learned $E_0$). % EV-217

The force of infection can be free or anchored.
A free rate exponentiates the read-out plus a learned bias, so the network must learn on its own the scale set by population and susceptibility.
The anchored rate supplies that scale,
\begin{equation}
\lambda^*_{i,h}=\frac{\max(c_{i,t-1},0.5)}{7\rho_{\rm eff}N_iS_i}
\exp\{\mathrm{clip}(r_{i,h},-10,10)\}.
\label{eq:anchor}
\end{equation}
% seirgnn2/models.py::Net._physics, lam_param == "anchor"; EV-172, EV-217
The first factor is the daily rate whose infections, reported at $\rho_{\rm eff}$, reproduce last week's count, so the read-out only has to learn a departure from it.
Both rates are multiplied by a learned spatial import term $\exp\{0.1\beta(u_i-\bar u)\}$, with $u_i=\log\max((AI)_i,10^{-9})$ from the border graph and $\bar u$ its mean over districts. % EV-217
A mass-action variant instead multiplies a learned daily transmission coefficient by the infectious fraction, recomputed each day, without the import term.
We call the adaptive encoder with the gated SEIR head, anchored rate, and learned $E_0$ the Adaptive SEIR-GNN.

\section{Experimental Setup}\label{sec:setup}
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/evaluation_protocol.pdf}
\caption{Evaluation protocol. At each of nine origins the model is trained on earlier windows, stopped early on 30 validation windows, and tested on the next 5\% of windows; seed-averaged origin scores are compared with persistence.}
\label{fig:protocol}
\end{figure}

We use rolling-origin evaluation (Fig.~\ref{fig:protocol}): the cut-off moves through the series, and the model is retrained at each origin.
The nine origins lie at 0.50 to 0.90 of the forecast-start list in steps of 0.05, and each test block covers the next 5\%. % EV-186
The 30 starts immediately before each cut-off form the validation set. % EV-182
We fixed this design after development runs with three origins (0.55, 0.70, 0.85; 15\% test blocks) and a wider nine-origin grid (0.40 + k/15). % EV-227
Three origins cannot give an exact sign-flip $p$ below 0.25, which motivated nine. % EV-181
Each learned model is trained with seeds 0, 1, and 2, giving 27 runs per model; persistence is deterministic. % EV-101

All models share one setting: Adam with learning rate 0.003 and weight decay 0.0001, batch size 32, cosine decay, gradient clipping at 5, up to 300 epochs, and early stopping on count-scale validation RMSE with patience 40. % EV-175, EV-224
Because every window forecasts three weeks, the last training and first validation targets share two weeks, as do the last validation and first test targets. % EV-218
We compare 30 learned models with persistence: GCN, LSTM, STGAT, A3T-GCN, ASTGCN, and AAGCN, each with direct, residual, and free-rate gated and bare SEIR heads, and six adaptive-encoder and anchored variants. % EV-179

Seeds are averaged within each origin, and each model is compared with persistence on the nine origin-level differences.
We report RMSE and MAE in cases per district-week, RMSE by horizon, the paired difference with a 95\% t interval, and the exact two-sided sign-flip test with Holm adjustment over the 30 models. % EV-200, EV-219
With nine origins the smallest attainable adjusted $p$ is 0.117, so the test can detect only differences that hold at every origin by a wide margin. % EV-226

\subsection{Comparison with persistence and baselines}
Table~\ref{tab:main} gives the test results.
Persistence has RMSE 28.54 and MAE 13.94; the GCN with a residual head, our baseline graph network, has 28.12 and 13.62. % EV-200, EV-202
The Adaptive SEIR-GNN has the lowest test RMSE of all models, 27.45, a paired difference from persistence of -1.10 with interval [-2.84, 0.65]. % EV-215
Its raw sign-flip $p$ is 0.199 and its Holm-adjusted $p$ is 1.000, so the improvement is not significant. % EV-219
No learned model differs significantly from persistence after adjustment, in either direction. % EV-219
Fig.~\ref{fig:forest} shows that the intervals of the strongest models all lie mostly below zero but include it.
Fig.~\ref{fig:origins} shows why: the Adaptive SEIR-GNN is below persistence at 7 of the 9 origins, but the origins differ far more from each other than the models do. % EV-114

\subsection{What the SEIR decoder contributes}
Fig.~\ref{fig:results}b compares the mechanistic heads.
On the GCN encoder, anchoring the force of infection lowers the gated SEIR head from 28.43 to 27.62. % EV-210, EV-213
Gating matters as much as anchoring: the bare anchored SEIR head on the adaptive encoder reaches 29.80, above persistence. % EV-211
The mass-action variant reaches 28.39, and the anchored gated head scores 27.45 with or without the learned $E_0$. % EV-212, EV-214, EV-215
The adaptive encoder with a residual head and no SEIR decoder scores 27.94. % EV-208
That comparison changes the head and the anchor together, so it does not isolate the SEIR equations.
On the three-origin protocol, a gated head without the simulator is within 0.68 of the gated SEIR head on validation for STGAT, A3T-GCN, and DCRNN, while the SEIR version has lower test error for all three. % EV-159, EV-160, EV-161

\subsection{Horizon and data quality}
The Adaptive SEIR-GNN is below persistence at every horizon, by 1.03, 0.86, and 1.38 cases (Fig.~\ref{fig:results}a). % EV-153
Persistence rises from 23.47 at one week to 33.26 at three weeks; the GCN residual baseline goes from 23.24 to 32.47. % EV-225
On the legacy array, removing the six windows that touch the erroneous row lowers mean persistence RMSE from 44.80 to 29.52, and the last fold alone from 68.62 to 22.80 (Fig.~\ref{fig:results}c). % EV-220
One spreadsheet error thus changes how hard the task appears by more than a third, while the best model differs from persistence by 1.10. % EV-220, EV-215

\section{Discussion and Limitations}\label{sec:discussion}
The SEIR decoder becomes useful once the force of infection carries the population and susceptible scale and a gate lets the model fall back on last week's count.
Without the anchor, the head must learn a district-specific scale it never sees; without the gate, a bare simulator overshoots or undershoots and loses to persistence.
We believe this is why the anchored, gated decoder gives the lowest errors, but the experiments do not separate the contribution of the SEIR equations from that of the gate and anchor.
Persistence is likely hard to beat because weekly counts change slowly over three weeks, while a learned model must estimate its parameters from few epidemic regimes.

Several limitations apply.
The nine origins were chosen after development runs on other origin designs, and the six adaptive and anchored variants were added after earlier results were seen, so these results are development evidence, not confirmation on unseen weeks.
Two target weeks overlap at each partition boundary, which lets early stopping see some outcomes of the first test windows.
The graph used in the experiments has two entries that are not shared borders.
All models share one training setting rather than an equal tuning budget, so the weaker published encoders may be under-tuned.
The fixed rates, the reporting fraction, and the Colombo seroprevalence are assumptions, and the decoder has no serotypes, waning immunity, or mosquito compartment.
The study covers one country, one disease, and a three-week horizon. % EV-007
Our next step is an evaluation on weeks after February 2024 with the corrected graph, a matched gated head without SEIR, equal tuning, and seasonal and autoregressive baselines, all fixed in advance.

\section{Conclusion}
We proposed an SEIR-informed graph network for weekly district-level dengue forecasting in Sri Lanka.
Anchoring the force of infection to population and susceptibility, and gating the simulator with last week's count, gives the lowest test error among 30 models, 27.45 against 28.54 for persistence. % EV-200, EV-215
The gain is not significant on nine origins, and a single source-table error changes the baseline far more than the best model's gain. % EV-219, EV-220
Epidemic mechanics can be made to work inside a graph network; showing that they improve forecasts needs a longer, untouched test period.
